overview: This file documents the North Formosa Peace Memorial Association’s August 1941 arrangements for administering the proceeds from the sale of its property in Taihoku (present-day Taipei). American Vice Consul Glen Bruner forwarded an invitation to join the Association’s Board of Trustees, his qualified acceptance, and the minutes of an August 26 meeting to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo. The central issue was how the fund should be disposed of if no foreign trustee remained resident in Taiwan; the trustees unanimously assigned that future decision to the American and British embassies in Tokyo, acting with the head offices of the trustee firms.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting records of the North Formosa Peace Memorial Association
subfiles.from: Glen Bruner, American Vice Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Bruner transmits three enclosures concerning his membership on the Association’s Board of Trustees and its August 26 meeting.
subfiles.summary: Bruner forwards an invitation to membership, his reply, and signed minutes of the trustees’ meeting at the Twatutia Foreign Club. He suggests that any request for further information be directed to the British Embassy in Tokyo. The despatch records its distribution to the Embassy, the Department of State, the Consulate General at Tokyo, and the consular files.

subfiles.title: Invitation to serve on the Association’s Board of Trustees
subfiles.about: The Association invites the resident American consul to occupy a seat on the Board of Trustees.
subfiles.summary: The page’s OCR is effectively illegible, preserving only repeated instances of the year 1941. Its identity and date are supplied by the enclosing despatch, which describes Enclosure No. 1 as an invitation to membership dated August 19, 1941, and by Bruner’s reply on the following page. The invitation evidently explained that the Association’s property-sale proceeds had been entrusted to a five-member board that included the resident American consul.

subfiles.title: Glen Bruner’s qualified acceptance of trusteeship
subfiles.about: Bruner agrees to serve on the Board of Trustees only in a nonexecutive or advisory capacity consistent with Foreign Service practice.
subfiles.summary: Bruner acknowledges Orr’s notice that proceeds from the Association’s Taihoku property had been placed under a five-member Board of Trustees and that the resident American consul had been named a trustee. He accepts the invitation subject to the customary rule that American consular officers should not hold executive or quasi-executive posts in outside organizations. The printed OCR date of “August 10” is evidently a misreading or inconsistency, since the covering despatch dates the invitation August 19 and the reply calls Orr’s communication one “of even date.”

subfiles.title: Minutes of the Board of Trustees meeting
subfiles.from: R. B. Orr, Honorary Secretary and Treasurer
subfiles.to: Board of Trustees of the North Formosa Peace Memorial Association
subfiles.about: The trustees decide who should control disposition of the fund if no foreign trustee remains resident in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The board met at the Twatutia Foreign Club in Taihoku with W. W. McVittie, Glen Bruner, R. B. Orr, and F. H. Berger present. McVittie proposed, and Bruner seconded, that if no foreigner remained in Taihoku to act as trustee, the American and British embassies in Tokyo should decide how to dispose of the fund in consultation with the head offices of the trustee firms. The motion carried unanimously, and Orr signed the minutes as honorary secretary and treasurer.

interest: The file offers a compact view of foreign-community institutional life in colonial Taiwan immediately before the Pacific War. It is particularly useful for showing how American consular ethics limited participation in local organizations and how British and American officials planned for the possible disappearance of foreign residents from Taihoku. The contingency resolution, adopted only months before hostilities began between Japan and the United States and United Kingdom, gives the otherwise routine trustees’ minutes unusual historical resonance.
